{"id": "94f18449-cd5a-40f6-b186-e9c82bb0a08e", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_rVoUrJEN4Nk1OHI9wzLcez", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Reliability\",\"context\":\"## Dual on-premises sites with multiple DX connections example\\n\\nThe scenario illustrated in Figure 11 shows two on-premises data center sites located\\nin different geographical Regions, and connected to AWS using the Maximum Resiliency\\nconnectivity model (described in the AWS Direct Connect Resiliency\\nRecommendations) using AWS Direct Connect with DXGW and VGW. These two on-premises\\nsites are interconnected to each other over a data center interconnect (DCI) link. The\\non-premises IP prefixes (192.168.0.0/16) that belongs to remote branch sites are advertised\\nfrom both on-premises data center sites. The primary path for this prefix should be data\\ncenter 1. Traffic to and from the remote branch sites will failover to data center 2 in a\\nfailure event of data center 1 or both DX locations. Also, there is a site-specific IP\\nprefix for each data center. These prefixes need to be reached directly, and via the other\\ndata center site in case of both DX locations failure.\\n\\nBy associating BGP Community attributes with the routes advertised to AWS DXGW, you\\ncan influence the egress path selection from AWS DXGW side. These community attributes\\ncontrol AWS\u2019s BGP Local Preference attribute assigned to the advertised route. For more\\ninformation, refer to AWS DX Routing policies and BGP\\ncommunities.\\n\\nTo maximize the reliability of the connectivity at the AWS Region level, each pair of\\nAWS DX connections configures ECMP so that both can be utilized at the same time for data\\ntransfer between each on-premises site and AWS.\\n\\n*Figure 11 \u2013 Dual on-premises sites with multiple DX connections example*\\n\\nWith this design, the traffic flows destined to the on-premises networks (with the same\\nadvertised prefix length and BGP community) will be distributed across the dual DX\\nconnections per site using ECMP. However, if ECMP is not required across the DX connection,\\nthe same concept discussed earlier and described in the Routing policies and BGP\\ncommunities documentation can be used to further engineer the path selection at a\\nDX connection level.\\n\\nNote: If there are security devices in the path within the on-premises data centers,\\nthese devices need to be configured to allow traffic flows leaving over one DX link and\\ncoming from another DX link (both links utilized with ECMP) within the same data center\\nsite\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/hybrid-connectivity/reliability.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Traffic Segmentation Options in AWS Direct Connect\",\"context\":\"## Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN Attachments (Public VIFs) and AWS Direct Connect to Extend Your On-Premises VRFs diagram\\n\\nIf your customer gateway does not support Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE), you\\ncan still segment your traffic by creating one AWS Site-to-Site VPN\\nconnection per each VRF you have in your data center. You can use a public VIF as underlaying transport.\\n\\n1. Traffic initiated from an instance in Spoke VPC A and destined for the\\n corporate data center server (in VRF A) is routed to the Transit Gateway elastic\\n network interface (TGW ENI) according to the Spoke VPC A route table.\\n2. Traffic is forwarded to Transit Gateway. Traffic is then\\n routed to the corporate data center through Site-to-Site VPN connection\\n A according to the Segment A route table.\\n3. The Site-to-Site VPN connection is created using a public\\n VIF as transport (VLAN). The on-premises router must be configured\\n to use a different VPN connection per VRF configured.\\n4. The on-premises router forwards the traffic from Site-to-Site VPN\\n connection A to the VRF A and the destination server.\\n5. Traffic from the corporate data center\u2019s VRF B destined for Spoke VPC B is first\\n sent to the customer gateway located in the data center.\\n6. The customer gateway chooses Site-to-Site VPN connection B to\\n send the traffic to the Transit Gateway over\\n the Direct Connect link.\\n7. Traffic is forwarded to the Spoke VPC B attachment according to\\n the Transit Gateway Segment B route table.\\n8. The TGW ENI of Spoke VPC B forwards the traffic to the destination\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/reference-architecture-diagrams/latest/electronics-hpc/traffic-segmentation-aws-direct-connect.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"On-Premises Connectivity Using AWS Direct Connect to a Virtual Private Gateway and VPN\",\"context\":\"## VMware Cloud on AWS networking with Direct Connect to VGW architecture\\n\\nThe following numbered items describe the key components in this architecture:\\n\\n1. A private virtual interface (VIF) establishes connectivity to the VMware Software-defined Data Center (SDDC) A in AWS Region A.\\n2. An AWS Site-to-Site VPN (over internet) provides backup connectivity to the private VIF to provide resilient connectivity to the VMware SDDC A.\\n3. A public VIF enables access to all AWS public services and endpoints using public IP addresses.\\n4. The lack of an AWS Direct Connect connection in Region B creates a design constraint; therefore, a Site-to-Site VPN is established to the VMware SDDC B. This VPN uses the public VIF from the Direct Connect connection in Region A. Site-to-Site VPNs over a public VIF can be used to establish a more consistent network experience compared to internet-based VPNs.\\n5. A private VIF to the AWS Direct Connect gateway (DXGW) enables the DXGW to establish on-premises communication to Amazon VPCs in different Regions by associating the DXGW to the virtual private gateways (VGW).\\n6. The private VIF to DXGW cannot be used for gateway associations to a VMware SDDC. This feature is not supported on VMware Cloud on AWS.\\n7. Gateway associations are established between the DXGW and the VGW to enable on-premises communication with Amazon VPCs in multiple Regions.\\n8. Site-to-Site VPNs are configured as a backup to the DXGW-VGW associations for more resilient connectivity to Amazon VPCs\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/reference-architecture-diagrams/latest/vmware-cloud-networking/vmware-dx-vgw-vpn.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify whether two on-premises sites can communicate via separate Direct Connect VIFs"}

{"id": "2adbc28a-74d4-4cca-8c15-e6eab9e98d05", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_8IbFq8eNetSpZhRv1JyMKz", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Direct Connect virtual private gateway associations\",\"context\":\"# Direct Connect virtual private gateway associations\\n\\nYou can associate a virtual private gateway with a Direct Connect gateway to enable\\nconnectivity between your Direct Connect connection and VPCs across different accounts and\\nRegions. Each VPC requires a virtual private gateway that you associate with the Direct\\nConnect gateway. Once these associations are established, you create private virtual\\ninterfaces on your Direct Connect connection to the Direct Connect gateway, allowing\\nmultiple VPCs to share the same Direct Connect connection through their respective virtual\\nprivate gateway associations..\\n\\nThe following rules apply to virtual private gateway associations:\\n\\n* Do not enable route propagation until after you've associated a virtual\\n gateway with a Direct Connect gateway. If you enable route propagation before\\n associating the gateways, routes might be propagated incorrectly.\\n* There are limits for creating and using Direct Connect gateways. For more\\n information, see Direct Connect quotas.\\n* You cannot attach a Direct Connect gateway to a virtual private gateway when the\\n Direct Connect gateway is already associated with a Transit Gateway.\\n* The VPCs to which you connect through a Direct Connect gateway cannot have\\n overlapping CIDR blocks. If you add an IPv4 CIDR block to a VPC that's\\n associated with a Direct Connect gateway, ensure that the CIDR block does not\\n overlap with an existing CIDR block for any other associated VPC. For more\\n information, see Adding\\n IPv4 CIDR Blocks to a VPC in the\\n *Amazon VPC User Guide*.\\n* You cannot create a public virtual interface to a Direct Connect\\n gateway.\\n* A Direct Connect gateway supports communication between attached private virtual\\n interfaces and associated virtual private gateways only, and may enable a\\n virtual private gateway to another private gateway. The following traffic flows\\n are not supported:\\n\\n + Direct communication between the VPCs that are associated with a\\n single Direct Connect gateway. This includes traffic from one VPC to\\n another by using a hairpin through an on-premises network through a\\n single Direct Connect gateway.\\n + Direct communication between the virtual interfaces that are attached\\n to a single Direct Connect gateway.\\n + Direct communication between the virtual interfaces that are attached\\n to a single Direct Connect gateway and a VPN connection on a virtual\\n private gateway that's associated with the same Direct Connect\\n gateway.\\n* You cannot associate a virtual private gateway with more than one Direct\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/virtualgateways.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Direct Connect gateways and Transit Gateway associations\",\"context\":\"# Direct Connect gateways and Transit Gateway associations\\n\\nYou can use Direct Connect gateway to connect your Direct Connect connection over a transit virtual\\ninterface to the VPCs or VPNs that are attached to your Transit Gateway. You associate a Direct Connect\\ngateway with the Transit Gateway. Then, create a transit virtual interface for your Direct Connect connection\\nto the Direct Connect gateway.\\n\\nThe following rules apply to Transit Gateway associations:\\n\\n* You cannot attach a Direct Connect gateway to a Transit Gateway when the Direct Connect\\n gateway is already associated with a virtual private gateway or is attached to a\\n private virtual interface.\\n* There are limits for creating and using Direct Connect gateways. For more\\n information, see Direct Connect quotas.\\n* A Direct Connect gateway supports communication between attached transit virtual\\n interfaces and associated Transit Gateways.\\n* If you connect to multiple Transit Gateways that are in different Regions, use unique\\n ASNs for each Transit Gateway.\\n* Any point-to-point connectivity address using a `/30` range \u2014 for\\n example, `192.168.0.0/30` \u2014 does not propagate to a Transit Gateway\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-transit-gateways.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Why can't I use a Direct Connect connection to connect to VPC resources over a transit virtual interface?\",\"context\":\"### Review your transit gateway settings\\n\\nMake sure that you correctly configured your transit gateway settings:\\n\\n* Follow the [rules for transit gateway associations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-transit-gateways.html). Transit virtual interfaces use Direct Connect gateway associations with transit gateways to facilitate communication. This communication goes from the on-premises network to multiple VPCs in all AWS Regions and accounts over a single transit virtual interface. .\\n* Review your [transit gateway routing configuration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html#tgw-route-tables-overview). You can configure route tables to propagate routes for any attached VPCs, virtual private networks (VPNs), or Direct Connect connections. You can also add static routes to the transit gateway route tables. When a packet comes from one attachment, the packet uses the route table that matches the destination IP address to route to another attachment. \\n **Note:** You can associate only one route table with each attachment. However, an attachment can propagate its routes to more than one route table.\\n* If you attached a VPC to your transit gateway, then review your Availability Zones. Make sure that you select the appropriate number of Availability Zones for the transit gateway to route traffic to resources in VPC subnets. The transit gateway uses one IP address from the subnet to create a network interface in that subnet.\\n* For resources in different Availability Zones, confirm that the transit gateway elastic network interface is in that Availability Zone. \\n **Important:** Availability Zones that don't have a transit gateway attachment can't reach the transit gateway. If you can route traffic from one Availability Zone but not another, then review the transit gateway network interface. The transit gateway network interface must be in that zone. For high availability, it's a best practice to turn on transit gateway network interfaces in multiple Availability Zones\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-fix-connectivity-to-vpc\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify if Direct Connect Gateway or Transit Gateway allows traffic between two on-premises VIFs"}

{"id": "2a3267d5-2228-44da-8f66-89aad5195fba", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_X6QS84AqLBrKLXF2pEIUXD", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Traffic Segmentation Options in AWS Direct Connect\",\"context\":\"## Segment Your Traffic over AWS Direct Connect by Using Several Transit VIFs and Direct Connect Gateways diagram\\n\\nTransit Virtual Interfaces (VIFs) are used to access AWS Transit Gateway by way of\\nan Direct Connect gateway. Each VIF is configured with an unique virtual local\\narea network (VLAN) tag, which means you can segment your traffic by using\\none VIF per virtual routing and forwarding (VRF) you have in your data\\ncenter. Take into account the limits in the number of VIFs, depending\\nthe type of Direct Connect connection you have. {"id": "45b3916b-9d08-4009-a527-371a80da33aa", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Short answer: it depends on which Direct Connect architecture you're using.

**Private VIFs + Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) or Direct Connect Gateway (DXGW) associated to a VGW — No.**
AWS explicitly disallows this. The Direct Connect Gateway documentation states that "direct communication between the virtual interfaces that are attached to a single Direct Connect gateway" is **not supported** — there's no hairpinning between two VIFs (or between a VIF and a VPN on an associated VGW) through this model.

**Transit VIFs + Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway — Yes.**
A Transit Gateway doesn't have that hairpin restriction. If each on-premises site has its own transit VIF (optionally via its own DX Gateway), and both are attached to the same Transit Gateway, you can configure the TGW route tables so traffic flows from one DX attachment to the other. This is the same underlying mechanism AWS documents for routing between two VPCs over two separate transit VIFs through a TGW (often used to hairpin traffic through an on-prem firewall) — attachment-to-attachment routing works as long as the route tables permit it.

So to connect two on-prem sites through AWS, you'd want the transit VIF + Transit Gateway design, not a plain VGW/private-VIF setup.

Want me to look at how your account's Direct Connect gateways and Transit Gateway attachments are currently configured to see which model you're on?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
